fixes.explanation: That's it, friend. Neco, king of Egypt, is the one who makes Eliakim, the brother of Jehoahaz, king over Judah and Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 36:4). Egypt took the old king off the throne and then picked the next one too (2 Chronicles 36:3). A different hand put the crown on this time than in verse 1.

Egypt is right. Neco, king of Egypt, takes Jehoahaz and carries him off there (2 Chronicles 36:4). Jehoahaz had been Judah's king, and now he's headed to Egypt with Neco. That's a rough commute, friend.

That's right. Jehoiakim doesn't do what is right. The text says he "…did evil in the sight of the LORD his God." (2 Chronicles 36:5). Later the text says his abominations, and all that was found against him, are written in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah (2 Chronicles 36:8).

You've got it. Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, takes some of the articles from the house of the LORD to Babylon (2 Chronicles 36:7). The house of the LORD is the temple in Jerusalem. He had bound Jehoiakim to take him to Babylon (2 Chronicles 36:6), and now he takes things from that holy place too.

Gates make sense when an army is raiding a city, friend, but the text doesn't mention them here. It says Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, takes some of the articles from the house of the LORD to Babylon (2 Chronicles 36:7). Those are the things to look for: what belonged in the LORD's house.

True. The text says Jehoiachin "…did evil in the sight of the LORD…" (2 Chronicles 36:9). He's the son of Jehoiakim, and he reigned in his father's place (2 Chronicles 36:8). Another king, and the verdict is the same.

Eleven is a number that fits this chapter, but it belongs to other kings. Jehoiakim reigns eleven years, and so does Zedekiah (2 Chronicles 36:5, 11). Jehoiachin only gets three months and ten days (2 Chronicles 36:9).

Right. Zedekiah rebels against King Nebuchadnezzar, who had made him swear by God (2 Chronicles 36:13). Nebuchadnezzar is the king he turned on. The text also says he stiffened his neck and hardened his heart against turning to the LORD, the God of Israel.

That's not what the text says, friend. It says Zedekiah rebelled against King Nebuchadnezzar, who had made him swear by God (2 Chronicles 36:13). Rebelled is the word the text uses. It also says he stiffened his neck and hardened his heart against turning to the LORD.

The text doesn't mention an army here, baker. What it says is that Zedekiah rebelled against King Nebuchadnezzar, the one who had made him swear by God (2 Chronicles 36:13). Rebelled is the word to look for.

Isaiah is a name you may know, baker, but this passage doesn't name him here. The text says the seventy years were "…in fulfillment of the word of the LORD spoken through Jeremiah." (2 Chronicles 36:21). Jeremiah is the one this passage points to. Keep his name handy, because it comes back in verse 22.

Ezekiel is another name you may know, friend, but this passage doesn't name him. It says the seventy years were "…in fulfillment of the word of the LORD spoken through Jeremiah." (2 Chronicles 36:21). So the name to remember is Jeremiah. The text names him twice in a row.
